title: Dataset Complexity Shapes Finite-Distance Loss Geometry in Neural Networks
abstract: Finite datasets can share the same size and low-order statistics while differing strongly in structural complexity. We connect this dataset complexity to loss-landscape geometry by pairing local label mixing across neighborhood scales with local entropy around trained neural-network solutions. Adapted from the Franz--Parisi construction in spin-glass theory, local entropy measures the effective volume of low-loss, solution-like parameter configurations at each distance from a reference. We estimate it in finite networks using adaptive sequential Monte Carlo. In a controlled synthetic sweep, greater dataset complexity produces a larger decrease in local entropy near the reference. Farther away, its radial derivative becomes weak and nearly common across conditions. Dataset complexity therefore changes where the effective solution volume contracts, rather than making it decrease uniformly faster. Experiments on real image data show the same qualitative trend, with label randomization further amplifying the effect. These results show that dataset structure shapes how low-loss neighborhoods are organized across finite distances from trained solutions.
summary: This work connects the structural complexity of finite datasets to the geometry of the loss landscape in neural networks. By measuring local entropy, the authors show that dataset structure dictates how the effective volume of low-loss solutions contracts as one moves away from the trained parameters. This provides a deep theoretical insight into the relationship between data statistics and the underlying energy landscape organization.
main_problem: The study investigates how the structural complexity of a finite training dataset influences the geometry of the loss landscape in neural networks at finite distances from the trained solution.
main_result: Greater dataset complexity causes a non-uniform contraction of the effective solution volume (local entropy) near the solution, suggesting dataset structure dictates the organization of low-loss neighborhoods across finite distances.
method: The authors employ local entropy, inspired by spin-glass theory, to measure the effective volume of low-loss parameter configurations, estimating it using adaptive sequential Monte Carlo and deriving theoretical limits via replica methods.
model_or_system: The model involves fully connected feed-forward neural networks trained on datasets (like MNIST or synthetic 2D families). The analysis compares the dataset complexity, quantified by local label mixing, against the loss landscape geometry.
key_observables: Local entropy, radial derivative of local entropy, Multiscale Complexity (CMS), and the full radial-shell local entropy density ($\Phi_{RS}(r)$).
important_parameters: Dataset complexity (local label mixing), distance from reference solution ($r$), and regularization parameters ($\gamma, \lambda$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on adapting concepts from spin-glass theory (e.g., Franz-Parisi construction) and utilizes replica symmetry breaking (RS) ansatz in the theoretical derivations.
figures_summary: Figures schematically illustrate how dataset complexity affects finite-distance loss geometry, and one figure compares finite-N Monte Carlo estimates of local entropy against the thermodynamic limit.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the problem (dataset complexity vs. loss geometry) to developing theoretical tools (local entropy estimation via SMC and replica methods) and finally presenting results showing that dataset structure controls the contraction profile of the solution volume.
why_interesting: The connection between data structure (a classical ML concept) and the geometry of the energy landscape (a core concept in statistical mechanics and disordered systems) provides a powerful, non-trivial link between machine learning theory and condensed matter physics.
